section.title: Exponential growth and decay
section.p: Newton’s method used a tangent line to solve an equation. Linear approximation helped us decide how far to move.
But many models do not first give an equation like
They give a law about change.

A population grows because each individual helps create more individuals. A radioactive substance decays because each atom has a chance to decay. A bank account grows because interest is earned on the current balance. In each case, the rate of change is tied to the amount already present.
That leads to the simplest and most important differential equation:

subsection.title: The differential equation y'=ky
subsection.p: A differential equation is an equation involving an unknown function and one or more of its derivatives.
does not ask for a number y. It asks for a function y(t) whose derivative is always k times the function itself.
The constant k controls the model.
The units of k are important. If y is measured in grams and t in years, then

exercise.title: Why does y'=ky ask for a function rather than a number?

statement.p: A differential equation involves an unknown function and its derivative. In your own words, why is y'=ky a law about change rather than a formula for y, and why does the sign of k decide growth versus decay?

hint.p: The equation says the rate is always proportional to the amount present. The solutions are the functions y(t)=y_0e^{kt} that obey that law.

subsection.title: Half-life and doubling time
subsection.p: The constant k is not always the most natural way to describe exponential change.
For growth, we often describe a quantity by its doubling time: the time it takes to multiply by 2.
For decay, we often describe a quantity by its half-life: the time it takes to multiply by 1/2.

exercise.title: Why do exponential models have a constant doubling time or half-life?

statement.p: If y(t)=y_0e^{kt}, the time needed to double (when k>0) or to halve (when k<0) does not depend on the starting amount. In your own words, why is that a consequence of constant relative growth, rather than an extra assumption?

hint.p: Multiplying the current amount by a fixed factor is the same as adding a fixed amount of time, because the exponential turns addition in time into multiplication of size.

subsection.title: Newton’s law of cooling
subsection.p: Not every exponential model has the form
A hot cup of coffee in a room does not cool toward 0^\circ. It cools toward the room temperature.
The natural changing quantity is not the temperature T itself, but the temperature difference between the coffee and the room.

subsection.title: What exponential models assume
subsection.p: Exponential models are powerful because they are simple. Their simplicity is also their danger.
says that the relative rate of change is constant:
If that ratio is not constant, the model is not exponential.

paragraphs.title: Warning example
paragraphs.p: The quantity is increasing for t>0, but it is not growing exponentially. Its relative rate of change is
This depends on t. It is not constant.
So increasing does not mean exponential. Even fast increasing does not mean exponential. Exponential growth means constant relative growth.

note.title: How to recognize the exponential model
note.p: when its rate of change is proportional to its current amount.

paragraphs.p: Exponential growth is often a good first approximation. But it cannot continue forever in a world with limited space, food, money, or people. The next model keeps the early exponential behavior but builds in a ceiling.

exercise.title: Why must the relative rate be constant for a model to be exponential?

statement.p: The equation y'=ky says y'/y=k. A quantity can increase without being exponential. In your own words, why is a changing relative rate a warning that the exponential model is the wrong promise, even if the graph is rising?

hint.p: Exponential models are powerful because they are simple. Their simplicity is also their danger: if y'/y is not constant, the model is not exponential.
